'''''Oenothera biennis''''', the '''common evening-primrose''',<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17}}</ref> is a species of flowering plant in the family Onagraceae, [[native species|native]] to eastern and central North America, from Newfoundland west to Alberta, southeast to Florida, and southwest to Texas, and widely [[naturalisation (biology)|naturalized]] elsewhere in temperate and subtropical regions.<ref name=grin>{{GRIN | access-date = 17 December 2017}}</ref> '''Evening primrose oil''' is produced from the plant.<ref name="nccih">{{cite web |title=Evening primrose oil |url=https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/evening-primrose-oil |publisher=National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health, US National Institutes of Health |access-date=23 July 2026 |date=1 November 2024}}</ref>

==Common names==
The plant is known by various common names, such as ''evening star'', ''sundrop'', ''German rampion'', ''hog weed'', and ''fever-plant''.<ref name=grin/><ref>{{cite book | author=Blanchan, N. | title=Wild Flowers Worth Knowing | year=1922 | publisher=[[Project Gutenberg|Project Gutenberg Literary Archive Foundation]]| title-link=Wild Flowers Worth Knowing | author-link=Neltje Blanchan }}</ref>

==Description==
[[File:Illustration Oenothera biennis0.jpg|thumb|upright|Illustration of ''Oenothera biennis'']]
''Oenothera biennis'' usually has a life span of two years ([[biennial plant|biennial]]) growing to {{cvt|1.6|m}} tall in the seeding year.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|last1=Elias|first1=Thomas S.|title=Edible Wild Plants: A North American Field Guide to Over 200 Natural Foods|last2=Dykeman|first2=Peter A.|publisher=[[Sterling Publishing|Sterling]]|year=2009|isbn=978-1-4027-6715-9|location=New York|page=103|oclc=244766414|orig-date=1982}}</ref> The [[leaf|leaves]] are lanceolate, {{cvt|8|-|18|cm|0}} long and {{cvt|2|-|6|cm|frac=4}} wide,<ref name=":0" /> produced in a tight [[Rosette (botany)|rosette]] the first year, and spirally on a stem the second year. However, plants with annual life cycles are documented, and have been selected for under experimental conditions  in environments with low competition.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Agrawal |first1=Anurag A. |last2=Johnson |first2=Mark T.J. |last3=Hastings |first3=Amy P. |last4=Maron |first4=John L. |title=A Field Experiment Demonstrating Plant Life-History Evolution and Its Eco-Evolutionary Feedback to Seed Predator Populations |journal=The American Naturalist |date=2013 |volume=181|issue=S1 |pages=S35-45 |doi=10.1086/666727 |pmid=23598358 |bibcode=2013ANat..181S..35A |hdl=1813/66733 |s2cid=15852492 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

===Growing cycle===
Most commonly, ''O. biennis'' grows as a low, spreading herb in the first year, just a few centimetres tall, with its leaves spreading out in a rosette to cover the ground, whilst storing energy in a thick root. In the second year, it grows up much taller, to around {{convert|1.6|m|ft}} tall, on a semi-woody stem, which then flowers and seeds. This will usually die at first frosts, but occasionally grows another stem in the third year.

===Blooming and fruiting===
Blooming lasts from late spring to late summer. The flowers are [[hermaphrodite (botany)|hermaphrodite]], produced on a tall spike and only last until the following noon. They open visibly fast every evening producing an interesting spectacle, hence the name "evening primrose".

The blooms are yellow, {{cvt|2.5|-|5|cm|frac=4}} diameter, with four bilobed [[petal]]s. The flower structure has a bright [[nectar guide]] pattern, invisible to the naked eye. This pattern is apparent under ultraviolet light and visible to its [[pollination|pollinators]], moths, butterflies, and bees.

The fruit is a [[capsule (fruit)|capsule]] {{cvt|2|-|4|cm|frac=4}} long and {{cvt|4|-|6|mm|2}} broad, containing numerous {{cvt|1|-|2|mm|2}} long [[seed]]s, released when the capsule splits into four sections at maturity.<ref name=borealforest>Borealforest: [http://www.borealforest.org/world/herbs_shrubs/common_evening_primrose.htm ''Oenothera biennis''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070713162913/http://www.borealforest.org/world/herbs_shrubs/common_evening_primrose.htm |date=2007-07-13 }}</ref><ref name=bc>Plants of British Columbia: [http://linnet.geog.ubc.ca/Atlas/Atlas.aspx?sciname=Oenothera+biennis ''Oenothera biennis''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161221013545/http://linnet.geog.ubc.ca/Atlas/Atlas.aspx?sciname=Oenothera+biennis |date=2016-12-21 }}</ref><ref name=jeps>Jepson Flora: [http://ucjeps.berkeley.edu/cgi-bin/get_JM_treatment.pl?Oenothera+biennis ''Oenothera biennis''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060918015022/http://ucjeps.berkeley.edu/cgi-bin/get_JM_treatment.pl?Oenothera+biennis |date=2006-09-18 }}</ref><ref name=uvf>Ultraviolet Flowers: [http://www.naturfotograf.com/UV_OENO_BIE.html ''Oenothera biennis''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061114102012/http://www.naturfotograf.com/UV_OENO_BIE.html |date=2006-11-14 }}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
''Oenothera biennis'' was given its [[scientific name]] in 1753 by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in the book ''[[Species Plantarum]]''. It has no accepted [[subspecies]] or [[Variety (botany)|varieties]], but it has {{table row counter|id=Synonyms}} [[Synonym (botany)|synonyms]] according to [[Plants of the World Online]].<ref name="POWO" />

==Ecology==
This plant is a weedy species that favors [[Disturbance (ecology)|disturbed]] environments.<ref name="illinois">{{cite web |title=Common Evening Primrose (Oenothera biennis) |url=https://www.illinoiswildflowers.info/prairie/plantx/cm_primrosex.htm |website=illinoiswildflowers.info}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Oenothera biennis (Evening Primrose) |url=https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/oenothera-biennis/ |website=plants.ces.ncsu.edu |publisher=NC State Extension}}</ref> It has been introduced and become established on all continents except Antarctica.<ref name="steck">{{cite journal |last1=Steckel |first1=Lawrence E. |last2=Sosnoskie |first2=Lynn M. |last3=Steckel |first3=Sandra J. |title=Common evening-primrose (''Oenothera biennis'' L.) |journal=Weed Technology |date=2019 |volume=33 |issue=5|pages=757–760 |doi=10.1017/wet.2019.53 |bibcode=2019WeedT..33..757S |s2cid=203879053 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

The seeds of the plant are important food for birds,<ref name=LBJ>{{NPIN|OEBI |access-date=7 December 2014}}</ref> including American goldfinch, Northern bobwhite, and mourning dove, and it is a larval host for both the [[primrose moth]] and the [[Hyles lineata|white-lined sphinx moth]].<ref>The Xerces Society (2016), ''Gardening for Butterflies: How You Can Attract and Protect Beautiful, Beneficial Insects'', Timber Press.</ref> Bumblebees and honeybees also visit the flowers.<ref name=illinois/>

The primrose moth (''Schinia florida'') is a common consumer of ''Oenothera biennis''.  The adults lay eggs on the flower, and the emerging caterpillars feed on the plant.
[[File:Animal insect Lepidoptera Schinia florida primose moth Oenothera 38 L Plymouth MA USA D 240724.jpg|thumb|Primrose moth, ''Schinia florida'', on an evening primrose; petals have been removed to reveal the insect]]

The seeds of ''O. biennis'' can remain viable in the [[soil seed bank]] for 70 years or more.<ref name=illinois/><ref name=steck/>

==Uses==

Over the centuries, [[Indigenous peoples|Indigenous people]] in North America have used the plant as food and [[traditional medicine]].<ref name=nccih/><ref name="ref1">{{cite journal|last1=Immel|first1=D.L.|title=Common evening primrose|url=https://plants.usda.gov/DocumentLibrary/plantguide/pdf/pg_oebi.pdf |journal=United States Department of Agriculture, National Plant Data Center|date=21 June 2001}}</ref>

The evening primrose was introduced to Europe in the early [[17th century]] as an ornamental plant in botanical gardens where its flowers are favored for [[nectar]] by pollinators, such as bees, and its seeds are food for birds.<ref name=nccih/><ref name="ref1"/>

===Food uses===
Most of the plant parts are edible, having a taste that is mild.<ref name="ref1"/> The roots can be eaten raw or cooked like potatoes.<ref name="ref1"/> The leaves can be eaten raw in salads or cooked like spinach or in soups.<ref name="ref1" /> Anishinaabe tribes traditionally make tea from the evening primrose leaves for use as a dietary aid and to reduce fatigue.<ref name="ref1" />

The flowering stems are preferably used when they are still young in June. They have to be peeled and can then be eaten raw or fried. The flower buds are regarded as a delicacy and can be harvested from June to October.<ref name="ref1"/>

The seeds have a protein content of about 15%, an oil content of 24%, and contain about 43% cellulose.<ref name="ref6">{{cite journal|last1=Hudson|first1=B.|title=Evening primrose (Oenothera spp.) oil and seed|journal=Journal of the American Oil Chemists' Society|date=1984|volume=61|issue=3|pages=540–543|doi=10.1007/bf02677026|s2cid=85005706}}</ref> The proteins are especially rich in the sulphur-containing [[amino acid]]s, [[methionine]] and [[cysteine]], and [[tryptophan]].<ref name="ref6" /><ref name="ref7">{{cite journal|last1=Brosnan|first1=J.T.|last2=Brosnan|first2=M.E.|title=The sulfur-containing amino acids: an overview|journal=The Journal of Nutrition|date=2006|volume=136|issue=6|pages=1636S–1640S|doi=10.1093/jn/136.6.1636s|pmid=16702333|doi-access=free}}</ref> [[Gamma-linolenic acid]] (GLA), and [[linoleic acid]] are present.<ref name="ref1" /><ref name="ref8">{{cite journal|last1=Ghasemnezhad|first1=A.|last2=Honermeier|first2=B.|title=Yield, oil constituents, and protein content of evening primrose (Oenothera biennis L.) seeds depending on harvest time, harvest method and nitrogen application|journal=Industrial Crops and Products|date=2008|volume=28|issue=1|pages=17–23|doi=10.1016/j.indcrop.2007.12.006}}</ref><ref name="ref9">{{cite journal|last1=Ghasemnezhad|first1=A.|last2=Honermeier|first2=B.|title=Seed yield, oil content and fatty acid composition of ''Oenothera biennis'' L. affected by harvest date and harvest method|journal=Industrial Crops and Products|date=2007|volume=25|issue=3|pages=274–281|doi=10.1016/j.indcrop.2006.12.005}}</ref> Mainly for these [[polyunsaturated]] [[fatty acid]]s, evening primrose oil is sold as a [[dietary supplement]].<ref name="ref1"/>

===Research===
{{See also|Gamma-Linolenic acid}}
There is not enough [[evidence-based medicine|clinical evidence]] to support the use of evening primrose oil as a therapy for any medical condition.<ref name=nccih/> A Cochrane review concluded that there was no effect of primrose oil on [[eczema]].<ref name="Cochrane - Evening primrose oil on ecezma">{{cite journal|last1=Bamford|first1=Joel|title=Oral evening primrose oil and borage oil for eczema|journal=Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews|date=30 April 2013|volume=2013|issue=4|doi=10.1002/14651858.CD004416.pub2|ref=Cochrane|pmid=23633319|article-number=CD004416|pmc=8105655}}</ref> The [[Mayo Clinic]] stated there was no good evidence that it affected eczema, [[diabetic neuropathy]] or [[premenstrual syndrome]].<ref name=mayo>{{Cite web |url=https://www.mayoclinic.org/drugs-supplements/evening-primrose/evidence/hrb-20059889 |title= Evening primrose (Oenothera spp.) |publisher=Mayo Clinic |date=13 November 2020|access-date=3 August 2022 }}</ref>

The [[American Cancer Society]] stated that there was little evidence for its effectiveness as an [[Cancer prevention|anti-cancer agent]], for which it is sometimes promoted, and "neither GLA nor other GLA-rich supplements (such as evening primrose oil) have been convincingly shown to be useful in preventing or treating any other health conditions."<ref name="acs">{{cite web|date=13 May 2010|title=Gamma linolenic acid|url=http://www.cancer.org/treatment/treatmentsandsideeffects/complementaryandalternativemedicine/pharmacologicalandbiologicaltreatment/gamma-linolenic-acid|access-date=1 August 2013|publisher=[[American Cancer Society]]|archive-date=6 August 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130806190429/http://www.cancer.org/treatment/treatmentsandsideeffects/complementaryandalternativemedicine/pharmacologicalandbiologicaltreatment/gamma-linolenic-acid|url-status=live}}</ref>

====Adverse effects====
Evening primrose oil is considered likely as safe in recommended doses.<ref name=nccih/><ref name=mayo/> It may increase the risk of bleeding, a concern for patients with bleeding disorders or taking drugs that may increase bleeding.<ref name=nccih/> The Mayo Clinic recommends caution in people with seizure disorders or mania, and by pregnant or breastfeeding women, and publishes a long list of possible [[side-effects]].<ref name=mayo/> Oral use of evening primrose oil may cause headaches or [[nausea]].<ref name=mayo/>

==== Traditional medicine====
The leaves and stems were used by [[Native Americans in the United States|Native Americans]] to treat skin, digestion, and [[sore throat|throat]] conditions.<ref name=nccih/>

==Agricultural practices==
The knowledge of agricultural practices in the cultivation of evening primrose is relatively new and only pertain to the commercialized production of evening primrose seed oil. Information of agricultural practices for the production of root vegetable or other plant parts is not known yet.

The evening primrose prefers sunny and arid places with loamy soil and occurs below {{convert|700|m|ft|-1}} above sea level.<ref name="ref1" /> One important prerequisite is to meet adequate nitrogen requirements. While too high nitrogen levels could lead to a quality and quantity decline of the oil content in the seeds, moderate nitrogen levels lead to increased seed quality and quantity.<ref name="ref8" /> Because the evening primrose is a light-dependent germinator, it is important that the seeds are not planted too deep into the soil, about {{convert|0.5|–|1.0|cm|1}} deep. The cultivation of evening primrose is thus suitable for [[no-till farming]], but the plants require an intense mechanical weed control. The seeds are tiny, about {{convert|0.3|-|0.7|g}}. They need approximately two to three weeks to germinate and are therefore very susceptible to the outgrowth of weeds.

Evening primrose seeds can be sown in the first half of April (spring seeds) or from mid-July to mid-August (autumn seeds).<ref name="ref1" /><ref name="ref8" /> The time of harvest is approximately 75 to 80 days (spring seeds) or 100 days (autumn seeds) after flowering, and clearly influenced by the plant variety, climate conditions, soil fertility and sowing time.<ref name="ref8" /><ref name="ref9" /> The population development and thus seed maturation of the evening primrose is very heterogeneous which is a rather difficult production factor.<ref name="ref1" />

There is not much water needed during the vegetation period.<ref name="ref1" /> A study has shown, that the irrigation with salt water could increase the oil yield and quality in evening primrose seeds. This might be a great opportunity especially in regions with limited water resources. Thus, the evening primrose could be a valuable alternative oil crop in arid regions.<ref name="ref1" />

Finally, the cultivation of evening primrose requires a proper field management otherwise the plant can become invasive.<ref name="ref1" /> If the seeds are used for pharmaceutical purposes it is also  important to grow the evening primrose without any pesticides to avoid any chemical residues.<ref name="ref1" />
